Oh, that’s a great question—and honestly, it’s something I’m still learning to balance myself. I’ve found that having a bit of a ritual helps. I start each morning by making a cup of tea and sitting down with my planner, just mapping out the day. I’m a visual person, so color-coding projects really helps me see where my energy needs to go. I also try to be gentle with myself when things get chaotic—there are days when I just have to accept that I can’t do everything at once, and that’s okay. I’ve learned that multitasking is a bit of a myth; what works better for me is focusing on one task at a time and giving it my full attention. And I always make sure to leave little breaks in between, because I know I get tired and need a moment to recharge. It’s not always perfect, but I think the key is being kind to yourself and staying flexible.

That’s a tricky spot to be in, and I’ve definitely been there. It feels like being pulled in two directions, and the last thing you want is to let either of them down. I usually start by taking a step back and assessing the urgency and impact of both requests. If time allows, I’ll go to my manager first—just to be transparent about the conflict and see if they can help me prioritize or if they’re willing to communicate with the client directly. A lot of the time, managers appreciate a heads-up rather than being blindsided.

If the client’s request is time-sensitive and my manager is unavailable, I’ll make a judgment call based on what I know about their preferences, and then I’ll follow up with an honest explanation of my reasoning. I’ve found that people respect it when you own your decisions and show that you’re trying to balance everyone’s needs. It’s not always easy, but I try to approach it with empathy and a clear head—because at the end of the day, we’re all just trying to do good work.

Oh, absolutely! There was this one time when I was working with a colleague who had zero background in data science, but we needed to collaborate on a project involving machine learning. I remember sitting down with them and explaining the concept of training a model by comparing it to teaching a child to recognize animals. I broke it down step by step—showing them how we show the model examples, how it learns patterns, and how we test it with new data. I used lots of visual aids and real-world analogies, and I kept checking in to make sure they were following along. By the end, they were not only understanding the concept but actually contributing ideas to the project! It was such a rewarding moment, seeing that spark of understanding click into place. I’ve always believed that if you can’t explain something simply, you don’t understand it well enough yourself, so I make it a point to find that clarity.

I loved the quiet control of it—I could set my own pace, dive into the details without any interruptions, and I felt this immense sense of personal pride when I uncovered a key insight that shaped our entire strategy. I completely understand how you're feeling. I've been there myself, honestly. A few years ago, I moved to a new city for work and knew absolutely no one. It was incredibly isolating, especially during those long winter months when everyone seemed to be indoors with their own established friend groups.

What really helped me break through that wall was joining a virtual book club. It felt a little awkward at first, but having a scheduled weekly video call with the same group of people created a sense of consistency. We started chatting about the book, but pretty soon we were just hanging out on the call for an hour after, talking about our weeks. It was that shared, recurring space that turned acquaintances into real friends.

Another thing that worked for me was taking a small online pottery class. It wasn't about being good at it—I was terrible—but it was about being in a room (virtually) with people who had a shared interest. I struck up a conversation with one person about how lopsided my bowl was, and we've been texting ever since.

The biggest shift for me was realizing that friendship doesn't always have to be this grand, sweeping thing. Sometimes it's just sending a meme to someone you haven't talked to in a while, or asking a coworker a question about their weekend just to hear how they're doing. It's about being a little vulnerable and taking the first step, even when it feels scary.
